claim: Arctic ground squirrels (AGS, Urocitellus parryii) survive harsh winter environmental conditions through hibernation.
source: Arctic ground squirrels (AGS, Urocitellus parryii) survive harsh winter environmental conditions through hibernation.
evidence: This is a well-established fact about AGS behavior and is supported by scientific knowledge about hibernating species.

claim: AGS body temperatures can drop below 0°C during hibernation.
source: By virtue of their profound ability to suppress metabolism and core temperature, with body temperatures dropping below 0°C, AGS are known as 'extreme' hibernators (Barnes, 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Barnes, 1989.

claim: Hibernation in AGS can last 7 months.
source: Hibernation in AGS can last 7 months and is characterized by drastic (>90%) reductions in basal metabolic rate, heart rate, and cerebral blood flow (Buck and Barnes, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Buck and Barnes, 2000.

claim: AGS hibernation is characterized by drastic (>90%) reductions in basal metabolic rate, heart rate, and cerebral blood flow.
source: Hibernation in AGS can last 7 months and is characterized by drastic (>90%) reductions in basal metabolic rate, heart rate, and cerebral blood flow (Buck and Barnes, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Buck and Barnes, 2000.

claim: Hibernation in AGS is interrupted periodically by interbout arousal (IBA) episodes in which temperature and cerebral blood flow normalize rapidly.
source: Curiously, hibernation is interrupted periodically by interbout arousal (IBA) episodes in which temperature and cerebral blood flow normalize rapidly (Drew et al., 2004; Karpovich et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Drew et al., 2004 and Karpovich et al., 2009.

claim: AGS suffer no ischemic injury during hibernation or reperfusion injury during an IBA.
source: Nonetheless, AGS suffer no ischemic injury during hibernation or reperfusion injury during an IBA.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the context of the manuscript discussing AGS resilience.

claim: Hibernating ground squirrels are resistant to ischemic and reperfusion injuries in numerous models, including brain and heart tissues after cardiac arrest in vivo and hippocampal slice models derived from animals during an IBA.
source: Hibernating ground squirrels are resistant to ischemic and reperfusion injuries in numerous models, including brain and heart tissues after cardiac arrest in vivo and hippocampal slice models derived from animals during an IBA (Dave et al., 2009; Quinones et al., 2016; Bhowmick et al., 2017; Bogren et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to Dave et al., 2009; Quinones et al., 2016; Bhowmick et al., 2017; Bogren et al., 2014.

claim: AGS resilience to reperfusion injury does not depend on temperature of the animal or season.
source: This resilience to reperfusion injury does not depend on temperature of the animal or season (Bhowmick et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bhowmick et al., 2017.

claim: AGS neural progenitor cells (NPCs) demonstrate resistance to oxygen and glucose deprivation ex vivo.
source: In addition, AGS neural progenitor cells (NPCs) demonstrate resistance to oxygen and glucose deprivation ex vivo (Drew et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Drew et al., 2016.

claim: AGS possess cell autonomous genetic mechanisms that contribute to intrinsic tolerance to metabolic stress or injury.
source: Together, these studies suggest that in addition to physiological adaptations, AGS possess cell autonomous genetic mechanisms that contribute to intrinsic tolerance to metabolic stress or injury.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the cited studies and the overall context of the manuscript.

claim: Post-translational modifications, regulation of cytoskeletal proteins, and upregulation of antioxidants play a prominent role in hibernating ground squirrel ischemia and hypothermia tolerance in the brain.
source: Although the mechanisms underlying hibernating ground squirrel ischemia and hypothermia tolerance in the brain are not fully elucidated, studies suggest that post-translational modifications, regulation of cytoskeletal proteins, and upregulation of antioxidants play a prominent role (Bhowmick and Drew, 2017; Lee et al., 2007; Tessier et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bhowmick and Drew, 2017; Lee et al., 2007; Tessier et al., 2019.

claim: Gene expression profiling and bioinformatic analyses indicate the cytoprotective contributions of mitochondrial and lysosomal pathways in adapting to hypothermia and hypoxia in ground squirrel and marmot species.
source: Gene expression profiling and bioinformatic analyses also indicate the cytoprotective contributions of mitochondrial and lysosomal pathways in adapting to hypothermia and hypoxia in ground squirrel and marmot species (Bai et al., 2019; Ou et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bai et al., 2019 and Ou et al., 2018.

claim: In neurons differentiated from 13-lined ground squirrel (13LGS) induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), hibernating ground squirrel microtubules retained stability upon exposure to hypothermia.
source: In neurons differentiated from 13-lined ground squirrel (13LGS) induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), Ou and colleagues found that hibernating ground squirrel microtubules retained stability upon exposure to hypothermia.
evidence: This claim is based on work by Ou and colleagues, which is cited in the manuscript.

claim: Mitochondrial suppression of cold-induced reactive oxygen species (ROS) and preservation of lysosomal structure are key features of ground squirrel cytoprotection.
source: The authors identified mitochondrial suppression of cold-induced reactive oxygen species (ROS) and preservation of lysosomal structure are key features of ground squirrel cytoprotection, and that pharmacological inhibition of ROS production or lysosomal proteases recapitulates the hypothermia-tolerant phenotype in human cells (Ou et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ou et al., 2018.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of ROS production or lysosomal proteases recapitulates the hypothermia-tolerant phenotype in human cells.
source: The authors identified mitochondrial suppression of cold-induced reactive oxygen species (ROS) and preservation of lysosomal structure are key features of ground squirrel cytoprotection, and that pharmacological inhibition of ROS production or lysosomal proteases recapitulates the hypothermia-tolerant phenotype in human cells (Ou et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ou et al., 2018.

claim: AGS and mouse NPCs exhibit similar morphology, growth rates and expression of Nestin and Ki67 when growing under identical cell culture conditions.
source: When growing under identical cell culture conditions, AGS and mouse NPCs exhibit similar morphology, growth rates and expression of Nestin and Ki67, markers for proliferating NPCs (Figure 1A–B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A-B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-E.

claim: AGS NPCs exhibit profound resistance to cell death compared with mouse NPCs when exposed to hypoxia (1% O2), hypothermia (31°C), or rotenone (30 µM).
source: When exposed to hypoxia (1% O2), hypothermia (31°C), or rotenone (30 µM), AGS NPCs exhibit profound resistance to cell death compared with mouse NPCs (Figure 1C), recapitulating resilient AGS phenotypes found in previous studies (Dave et al., 2009; Bhowmick et al., 2017; Bogren et al., 2014; Drew et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and citations to previous studies.

claim: AGS NPCs demonstrate strikingly higher 'spare respiratory capacity' in response to FCCP compared to mouse NPCs.
source: Moreover, measurement of in vitro oxygen consumption of AGS NPCs after sequential exposure to mitochondrial toxins demonstrates strikingly higher 'spare respiratory capacity' in response to FCCP (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, G), indicating a greater metabolic reserve for stressors (Nicholls and Budd, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, G, and a citation to Nicholls and Budd, 2000.

claim: Higher spare respiratory capacity indicates a greater metabolic reserve for stressors.
source: Moreover, measurement of in vitro oxygen consumption of AGS NPCs after sequential exposure to mitochondrial toxins demonstrates strikingly higher 'spare respiratory capacity' in response to FCCP (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, G), indicating a greater metabolic reserve for stressors (Nicholls and Budd, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nicholls and Budd, 2000.

claim: Mitochondrial citrate synthase and oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) enzymatic activities were similar between mouse and AGS NPCs, with the exception of complex IV.
source: Mitochondrial citrate synthase and oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) enzymatic activities were similar between the two species, with the exception of complex IV (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: At baseline, mouse and AGS cells had similar mitochondrial organization as evidenced by similar mean branch length and number of cells with fragmented mitochondria.
source: At baseline, mouse and AGS cells had similar mitochondrial organization as evidenced by similar mean branch length and number of cells with fragmented mitochondria (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Following FCCP treatment, mouse cells demonstrated marked increases in mitochondrial fission with concurrent decreases in mean branch length.
source: Following FCCP treatment, mouse cells demonstrated marked increases in mitochondrial fission with concurrent decreases in mean branch length.
evidence: This claim is based on data presented in the manuscript regarding mitochondrial morphology changes.

claim: AGS cells appeared largely resistant to mitochondrial fission induced by FCCP.
source: By contrast, AGS cells appeared largely resistant to mitochondrial fission induced by FCCP (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: A cDNA library expression screen identified a total of 378 putative cytoprotective genes from AGS NPCs.
source: We then isolated plasmids from surviving cells, amplified cDNA insert sequences by PCR and used next-generation sequencing to identify a total of 378 putative cytoprotective genes, three of which (Ags Atp5g1, Ags Manf, and Ags Calm1) provided cytoprotection in all three examined metabolic stress conditions (see Figure 2B and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the cDNA library screen and next-generation sequencing, shown in Figure 2B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Three genes (Ags Atp5g1, Ags Manf, and Ags Calm1) provided cytoprotection in all three examined metabolic stress conditions (hypoxia, hypothermia, and rotenone).
source: We then isolated plasmids from surviving cells, amplified cDNA insert sequences by PCR and used next-generation sequencing to identify a total of 378 putative cytoprotective genes, three of which (Ags Atp5g1, Ags Manf, and Ags Calm1) provided cytoprotection in all three examined metabolic stress conditions (see Figure 2B and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the cDNA library screen shown in Figure 2B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: ATP5G1 is one of three ATP5G isoforms making up the C-subunit of mitochondrial ATP synthases.
source: ATP5G1 is one of three ATP5G isoforms making up the C-subunit of mitochondrial ATP synthases, and is regulated distinctly from ATP5G2 or ATP5G3 (Gay and Walker, 1985; De Grassi et al., 2006; Wigington et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gay and Walker, 1985; De Grassi et al., 2006; Wigington et al., 2016.

claim: ATP5G1 is regulated distinctly from ATP5G2 or ATP5G3.
source: ATP5G1 is one of three ATP5G isoforms making up the C-subunit of mitochondrial ATP synthases, and is regulated distinctly from ATP5G2 or ATP5G3 (Gay and Walker, 1985; De Grassi et al., 2006; Wigington et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gay and Walker, 1985; De Grassi et al., 2006; Wigington et al., 2016.

claim: AGS ATP5G1 has three AGS-unique amino acid substitutions and two small insertions/deletions at the N-terminal region.
source: Based on multiple sequence alignment of the ATP5G1 protein family in mammals, we observed three AGS-unique amino acid substitutions and two small insertions/deletions at the N-terminal region of AGS ATP5G1, whereas the C-terminal membrane-spanning segment is largely invariant (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The C-terminal membrane-spanning segment of ATP5G1 is largely invariant across mammals.
source: Based on multiple sequence alignment of the ATP5G1 protein family in mammals, we observed three AGS-unique amino acid substitutions and two small insertions/deletions at the N-terminal region of AGS ATP5G1, whereas the C-terminal membrane-spanning segment is largely invariant (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The leucine-32 residue of AGS ATP5G1 in place of the otherwise highly conserved proline is unique to hibernating ground squirrels.
source: We found that the leucine-32 residue of AGS ATP5G1 in place of the otherwise highly conserved proline is unique to hibernating ground squirrels, and on conservation analysis scored among the highest of all AGS-unique amino acid substitutions in identified cytoprotective protein candidates from our screen (Andersson et al., 1997; Figure 2D and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by conservation analysis data shown in Figure 2D and Supplementary file 2, and a citation to Andersson et al., 1997.

claim: The leucine-32 substitution in AGS ATP5G1 scored among the highest of all AGS-unique amino acid substitutions in identified cytoprotective protein candidates on conservation analysis.
source: We found that the leucine-32 residue of AGS ATP5G1 in place of the otherwise highly conserved proline is unique to hibernating ground squirrels, and on conservation analysis scored among the highest of all AGS-unique amino acid substitutions in identified cytoprotective protein candidates from our screen (Andersson et al., 1997; Figure 2D and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by conservation analysis data shown in Figure 2D and Supplementary file 2.

claim: The N-terminal region of ATP5G proteins can undergo cleavage.
source: The N-terminal region of ATP5G proteins can undergo cleavage, but also modulate mitochondrial function directly, by unknown mechanisms (Vives-Bauza et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vives-Bauza et al., 2010.

claim: The N-terminal region of ATP5G proteins can modulate mitochondrial function directly, by unknown mechanisms.
source: The N-terminal region of ATP5G proteins can undergo cleavage, but also modulate mitochondrial function directly, by unknown mechanisms (Vives-Bauza et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vives-Bauza et al., 2010.

claim: The three C-subunit proteins (ATP5G1, ATP5G2, ATP5G3) are identical in sequence.
source: Although the three C-subunit proteins are identical in sequence, they cannot substitute for one another and are all required to constitute a fully functional C-subunit (Vives-Bauza et al., 2010; Sangawa et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Vives-Bauza et al., 2010 and Sangawa et al., 1997.

claim: The three C-subunit proteins (ATP5G1, ATP5G2, ATP5G3) cannot substitute for one another and are all required to constitute a fully functional C-subunit.
source: Although the three C-subunit proteins are identical in sequence, they cannot substitute for one another and are all required to constitute a fully functional C-subunit (Vives-Bauza et al., 2010; Sangawa et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Vives-Bauza et al., 2010 and Sangawa et al., 1997.

claim: In both mouse and AGS NPCs, expression of Atp5g3 or Atp5g2 is greater than that of Atp5g1.
source: We found that in both mouse and AGS NPCs, expression of Atp5g3 or Atp5g2 is greater than that of Atp5g1, consistent with prior reports in human and mouse tissues (Gay and Walker, 1985; Vives-Bauza et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data and citations to Gay and Walker, 1985 and Vives-Bauza et al., 2010.

claim: The relative abundance of the Atp5g1 isoform is elevated nearly twofold in AGS NPCs compared to mouse NPCs.
source: We found that the relative abundance of the Atp5g1 isoform is elevated nearly twofold in AGS NPCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The relative abundance of the mature ATP5G (subunit C) protein is not different in mouse and AGS cells.
source: However, the relative abundance of the mature ATP5G (subunit C) protein or oligomycin sensitivity of complex V activity, is not different in mouse and AGS cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E-F).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E-F.

claim: Oligomycin sensitivity of complex V activity is not different in mouse and AGS cells.
source: However, the relative abundance of the mature ATP5G (subunit C) protein or oligomycin sensitivity of complex V activity, is not different in mouse and AGS cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E-F).
evidence: This claim is supported by enzymatic activity data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E-F.

claim: Overexpression of the AGS variant of ATP5G1 in mouse NPCs confers cytoprotection in cells exposed to hypoxia, hypothermia, or rotenone.
source: Overexpression of the AGS variant of ATP5G1 in mouse NPCs confers cytoprotection in cells exposed to hypoxia, hypothermia, or rotenone (Figure 2E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell survival data shown in Figure 2E-G.

claim: The protective response of AGS ATP5G1 is not present in NPCs overexpressing ATP5G1L32P.
source: We found that this protective response is not present in NPCs overexpressing ATP5G1L32P.
evidence: This claim is based on cell survival data comparing AGS ATP5G1 and ATP5G1L32P.

claim: Overexpression of the human ATP5G1P32L leads to enhanced cytoprotection in metabolic stress conditions compared to that of human ATP5G1.
source: Conversely, overexpression of the human ATP5G1P32L, which mimics the wild-type AGS ATP5G1 variant, leads to enhanced cytoprotection in these conditions of metabolic stress compared to that of human ATP5G1.
evidence: This claim is based on cell survival data comparing human ATP5G1P32L and human ATP5G1.

claim: The ATP5G1 substitutions did not alter the mitochondrial localization of ATP5G1 when expressed in either mouse or AGS NPCs.
source: The ATP5G1 substitutions did not alter the mitochondrial localization of ATP5G1 when expressed in either mouse or AGS NPCs (Figure 3—figure supplements 1,2).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: Overexpression of the AGS variant of ATP5G1 increases spare respiratory capacity in mouse NPCs.
source: In addition, overexpression of the AGS variant of ATP5G1 recapitulated key features of the AGS resilient mitochondrial phenotype, including increasing spare respiratory capacity and reducing mitochondrial fission with reduced fragmentation and increased branch length of mitochondria in response to FCCP (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Seahorse data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Overexpression of the AGS variant of ATP5G1 reduces mitochondrial fission with reduced fragmentation and increased branch length of mitochondria in response to FCCP.
source: In addition, overexpression of the AGS variant of ATP5G1 recapitulated key features of the AGS resilient mitochondrial phenotype, including increasing spare respiratory capacity and reducing mitochondrial fission with reduced fragmentation and increased branch length of mitochondria in response to FCCP (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by mitochondrial morphology data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: NPCs expressing the AGS ATP5G1L32P variant demonstrated reduced spare respiratory capacity compared to the AGS ATP5G1 over-expressing NPCs.
source: Interestingly, NPCs expressing the AGS ATP5G1L32P variant demonstrated reduced spare respiratory capacity and increased mitochondrial fragmentation compared to the AGS ATP5G1 over-expressing NPCs.
evidence: This claim is based on Seahorse data comparing AGS ATP5G1 and AGS ATP5G1L32P.

claim: NPCs expressing the AGS ATP5G1L32P variant demonstrated increased mitochondrial fragmentation compared to the AGS ATP5G1 over-expressing NPCs.
source: Interestingly, NPCs expressing the AGS ATP5G1L32P variant demonstrated reduced spare respiratory capacity and increased mitochondrial fragmentation compared to the AGS ATP5G1 over-expressing NPCs.
evidence: This claim is based on mitochondrial morphology data comparing AGS ATP5G1 and AGS ATP5G1L32P.

claim: Overexpression of human ATP5G1P32L improved survival to metabolic stressors and reduced mitochondrial fragmentation.
source: Overexpression of human ATP5G1P32L improved survival to metabolic stressors and reduced mitochondrial fragmentation, but compared to AGS ATP5G1L32P spare respiratory capacity was not significantly improved.
evidence: This claim is based on cell survival and mitochondrial morphology data for human ATP5G1P32L.

claim: Compared to AGS ATP5G1L32P, human ATP5G1P32L spare respiratory capacity was not significantly improved.
source: Overexpression of human ATP5G1P32L improved survival to metabolic stressors and reduced mitochondrial fragmentation, but compared to AGS ATP5G1L32P spare respiratory capacity was not significantly improved.
evidence: This claim is based on Seahorse data comparing human ATP5G1P32L and AGS ATP5G1L32P.

claim: Improving spare respiratory capacity itself is not the sole mechanism conferring resilience to metabolic stressors.
source: This may indicate that improving spare respiratory capacity itself is not the sole mechanism conferring resilience to metabolic stressors.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that human ATP5G1P32L improved survival without significantly improving spare respiratory capacity.

claim: Expression of AGS ATP5G1 with two other identified AGS-unique amino acid substitutions (N34D, T39P) did not affect survival of mouse NPCs exposed to hypoxia, hypothermia, or rotenone.
source: Of note, expression of AGS ATP5G1 with two other identified AGS-unique amino acid substitutions (N34D, T39P) did not affect survival of mouse NPCs exposed to hypoxia, hypothermia, or rotenone (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell survival data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B-D.

claim: Using the adenine DNA base editor (ABEmax), AGS cell lines homozygous for ATP5G1L32P were successfully generated.
source: Using the recently reported adenine DNA base editor (ABEmax; 22), we successfully generated AGS cell lines homozygous for ATP5G1L32P by introducing a cytosine-to-thymine substitution in the (-) strand of Ags Atp5g1 (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: ABE KI cell lines did not demonstrate differences in Atp5g1 mRNA expression compared to ABEmax-treated AGS cells without successful knock-in.
source: Compared to ABEmax-treated AGS cells without successful knock-in (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), ABE KI cell lines did not demonstrate differences in Atp5g1 mRNA expression, protein abundance, or complex V activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-C, Figure 4I).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: ABE KI cell lines did not demonstrate differences in ATP5G1 protein abundance compared to ABEmax-treated AGS cells without successful knock-in.
source: Compared to ABEmax-treated AGS cells without successful knock-in (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), ABE KI cell lines did not demonstrate differences in Atp5g1 mRNA expression, protein abundance, or complex V activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-C, Figure 4I).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: ABE KI cell lines did not demonstrate differences in complex V activity compared to ABEmax-treated AGS cells without successful knock-in.
source: Compared to ABEmax-treated AGS cells without successful knock-in (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), ABE KI cell lines did not demonstrate differences in Atp5g1 mRNA expression, protein abundance, or complex V activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-C, Figure 4I).
evidence: This claim is supported by enzymatic activity data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Knock-in of the L32P residue resulted in markedly reduced survival of AGS NPCs following exposure to hypoxia, hypothermia, or rotenone.
source: However, knock-in of the L32P residue resulted in markedly reduced survival of AGS NPCs following exposure to hypoxia, hypothermia, or rotenone (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell survival data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: ABE KI AGS NPCs exhibited marked reduction in 'spare respiratory capacity' in response to FCCP treatment.
source: In addition, we found the ABE KI AGS NPCs exhibited marked reduction in 'spare respiratory capacity' and altered mitochondrial dynamics in response to FCCP treatment (Figure 4D–H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Seahorse data shown in Figure 4D-H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: ABE KI AGS NPCs exhibited altered mitochondrial dynamics in response to FCCP treatment.
source: In addition, we found the ABE KI AGS NPCs exhibited marked reduction in 'spare respiratory capacity' and altered mitochondrial dynamics in response to FCCP treatment (Figure 4D–H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by mitochondrial morphology data shown in Figure 4D-H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Overall ATP5G protein abundance is unchanged in ABE KI cells compared to ABE WT cells.
source: Although overall ATP5G protein abundance is unchanged (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D-E), we used clear-native gel electrophoresis (Kovalčíková et al., 2019; Wittig and Schägger, 2009) and identified a reduced presence of ATP synthase dimers relative to the total amount of ATP synthase in ABE KI cells (Figure 4J–K).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D-E.

claim: ABE KI cells show a reduced presence of ATP synthase dimers relative to the total amount of ATP synthase.
source: Although overall ATP5G protein abundance is unchanged (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D-E), we used clear-native gel electrophoresis (Kovalčíková et al., 2019; Wittig and Schägger, 2009) and identified a reduced presence of ATP synthase dimers relative to the total amount of ATP synthase in ABE KI cells (Figure 4J–K).
evidence: This claim is supported by clear-native gel electrophoresis data shown in Figure 4J-K.

claim: CRISPR edited ATP5G1L32P did not fully abolish the metabolic resilience phenotype in AGS NPCs.
source: CRISPR edited ATP5G1L32P did not fully abolish the metabolic resilience phenotype in AGS NPCs, indicating that other gene variants may also be involved.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that ABE KI cells still showed some resilience to metabolic stress.

claim: Other gene variants may also be involved in the metabolic resilience phenotype in AGS NPCs.
source: CRISPR edited ATP5G1L32P did not fully abolish the metabolic resilience phenotype in AGS NPCs, indicating that other gene variants may also be involved.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that ABE KI cells still showed some resilience to metabolic stress.

claim: Mitochondrial metabolic dysfunction is central to ischemia and reperfusion injury.
source: Mitochondrial metabolic dysfunction is central to ischemia and reperfusion injury.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field of ischemia and reperfusion injury research.

claim: Physiologic, transcriptomic, and proteomic studies have highlighted the importance of ketone and fatty acid metabolism in hibernating states.
source: Physiologic, transcriptomic, and proteomic studies have highlighted the importance of ketone and fatty acid metabolism in hibernating states (Brown and Staples, 2014; Xu et al., 2013) as well as pointed to a role for specific post-translational protein modifications in the differential regulation of metabolic pathways in hibernation (Ballinger et al., 2016; Chung et al., 2013; Herinckx et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Brown and Staples, 2014 and Xu et al., 2013.

claim: Specific post-translational protein modifications play a role in the differential regulation of metabolic pathways in hibernation.
source: Physiologic, transcriptomic, and proteomic studies have highlighted the importance of ketone and fatty acid metabolism in hibernating states (Brown and Staples, 2014; Xu et al., 2013) as well as pointed to a role for specific post-translational protein modifications in the differential regulation of metabolic pathways in hibernation (Ballinger et al., 2016; Chung et al., 2013; Herinckx et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ballinger et al., 2016; Chung et al., 2013; Herinckx et al., 2017.

claim: Specific variants of neuroprotective proteins have been identified to be upregulated in ground squirrels during hibernation including s-humanin.
source: Specific variants of neuroprotective proteins have also been identified to be upregulated in ground squirrels during hibernation including s-humanin, however, the phenotypic or mechanistic consequences of these variants are not known (Szereszewski and Storey, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Szereszewski and Storey, 2019.

claim: The phenotypic or mechanistic consequences of s-humanin variants in ground squirrels are not known.
source: Specific variants of neuroprotective proteins have also been identified to be upregulated in ground squirrels during hibernation including s-humanin, however, the phenotypic or mechanistic consequences of these variants are not known (Szereszewski and Storey, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Szereszewski and Storey, 2019.

claim: Altered mitochondrial dynamics and enhanced spare respiratory capacity in cells of AGS are potentially adaptive cellular mechanisms in hibernating animals.
source: We expanded this body of knowledge, by identifying altered mitochondrial dynamics and enhanced spare respiratory capacity in cells of AGS as potentially adaptive cellular mechanisms in hibernating animals.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The mitochondrial phenotype of AGS is likely responsible for the broad resilience of AGS cells against a wide range of metabolic stressors.
source: This mitochondrial phenotype is likely responsible for the broad resilience of AGS cells against a wide range of metabolic stressors.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Spare respiratory capacity, as measured by FCCP-stimulated oxygen consumption, represents a marker for cellular metabolic reserves.
source: Spare respiratory capacity, as measured by FCCP-stimulated oxygen consumption, represents a marker for cellular metabolic reserves, correlates with metabolic resilience (Nicholls and Budd, 2000) and is thought to be determined by the oxidative phosphorylation machinery (Pfleger et al., 2015; Yadava and Nicholls, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nicholls and Budd, 2000; Pfleger et al., 2015; Yadava and Nicholls, 2007.

claim: Spare respiratory capacity correlates with metabolic resilience.
source: Spare respiratory capacity, as measured by FCCP-stimulated oxygen consumption, represents a marker for cellular metabolic reserves, correlates with metabolic resilience (Nicholls and Budd, 2000) and is thought to be determined by the oxidative phosphorylation machinery (Pfleger et al., 2015; Yadava and Nicholls, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nicholls and Budd, 2000.

claim: Spare respiratory capacity is thought to be determined by the oxidative phosphorylation machinery.
source: Spare respiratory capacity, as measured by FCCP-stimulated oxygen consumption, represents a marker for cellular metabolic reserves, correlates with metabolic resilience (Nicholls and Budd, 2000) and is thought to be determined by the oxidative phosphorylation machinery (Pfleger et al., 2015; Yadava and Nicholls, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pfleger et al., 2015 and Yadava and Nicholls, 2007.

claim: Human and mouse NPCs and neural cells have been reported to have diminished spare respiratory capacity as they may respire maximally at baseline.
source: Notably, human and mouse NPCs and neural cells have been reported to have diminished spare respiratory capacity as they may respire maximally at baseline (Khacho et al., 2016; Lorenz et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Khacho et al., 2016 and Lorenz et al., 2017.

claim: AGS demonstrate marked elevations in spare respiratory capacity compared to mouse cells.
source: However, AGS demonstrate marked elevations in spare respiratory capacity compared to mouse cells, which likely explains marked AGS NPC survival even under complex I inhibition by rotenone (Yadava and Nicholls, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript and a citation to Yadava and Nicholls, 2007.

claim: Increased abundance of the Atp5g1 transcript in AGS compared with mouse NPCs could contribute to the altered mitochondrial function.
